paragraphs: Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi calls R’ Chiya “Ayya” in [Moed Katan 16b](https://www.sefaria.org/Moed_Katan.16b.2). In [Keritot 8a](https://www.sefaria.org/Keritot.8a.4), Bar Kappara uses the same nickname for R’ Chiya in conversation with Rabbi Hoshaya. As Hyman explains in his article on R’ Chiya, he understands the nickname as an allusion to Chiya’s difficulty pronouncing chet.[^1][^2][^3]

notes.text: [Rashi](https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Keritot.8a.4.2) explains that Bar Kappara uses Ayya as a term of disparagement.

The [short printed notice](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/ba/Aaron_Hyman._Toldoth_Tannaim_veAmoraim._III._1910.pdf#page=148) leaves the subject of the pronunciation clause implicit. Hyman’s [longer article on Chiya](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/60/Aaron_Hyman._Toldoth_Tannaim_veAmoraim._II._1910.pdf#page=10) assigns the difficulty to Chiya.

In a separate exchange in [Megillah 24b](https://www.sefaria.org/Megillah.24b.11), Rabbi tells his son Shimon to answer Chiya with a verse beginning vechikkiti. The Davidson edition explains the retort through the distinction between chet and heh.
